particulars: All names, dates, places, ages, counts (stab wounds, confessions, days, years, sentence lengths) and the specific governors, firm and inmates are omitted by design.

items.record: The case is a criminal prosecution of one man for rape and murder, carried through to a death sentence: "The jurors returned with their verdict of death."
items.reading: A corporation or public agency issues a press statement in reply to online critics about data, safety or policy.
items.loss: The basic kind of event and arena (a capital criminal case run by state justice institutions) is misidentified.

items.record: The 'manufactured account' is a coerced confession built through repeated police coaching: "Only on the fourth attempt at a rehearsed confession did authorities accept Washington's statement."
items.reading: A polished institutional explainer that is true line by line but misleading through framing and omission.
items.loss: The mechanism of fabrication (officials shaping a vulnerable person's words into a confession, not spin in a public statement) is misdescribed.

items.record: The confession contradicted the known facts and authorities overrode the gaps: "did not know the race of his victim, the address... or that he had raped her"; police "had to help him pick out Williams' apartment."
items.reading: Each sentence would likely hold up on review.
items.loss: The record shows outright factual falsity covered over by officials, not selective accuracy.

items.record: The accused was intellectually disabled and deferred to authority: "Washington would politely defer to any authority figure with whom he came into contact."
items.reading: The weaker party is a loosely organized fringe group of researchers, users or whistleblowers.
items.loss: The vulnerable party's position (a single cognitively disabled individual in custody, whose compliance was exploited) is missed.

items.record: Exculpatory forensic evidence was quietly altered once a suspect existed: "an amended forensic report was prepared (without additional testing being conducted) that said testing for the rare protein was 'inconclusive.'"
items.reading: Suppression is speculated as takedowns, NDAs, firings or legal threats, or simply crowding out critics with an authoritative account.
items.loss: The concrete suppression mechanism (tampering with scientific evidence to fit an already chosen suspect) is absent.

items.record: The trial was one-sided: "only the State's psychologist testified" and "the defense did not offer any counter argument to the jury concerning a sentence of death."
items.loss: The failure of the adversarial process and of defense counsel is missing.

items.record: Rescue came from fellow prisoners and volunteers inside the prison, not a public uproar: "another death row inmate... alerted Marie Deans (a non-lawyer...) and a lawyer... at the Virginia prison working on another case."
items.reading: A fringe concern spreads exponentially and virally through scattered individuals online.
items.loss: How the challenge actually spread (a chance chain of personal contacts among inmates, a volunteer and a lawyer, leading to a stay days before execution) is misdescribed.

items.record: Proof of innocence was blocked by a procedural deadline: "time barred by Virginia law, which allowed a defendant only 21 days to introduce new evidence, he was not exonerated."
items.loss: The legal rule that kept exculpatory DNA evidence from freeing him is missing.

items.record: Resolution came in slow, partial steps through executive clemency: commutation to life, then a limited pardon "on limited grounds that a jury would not have convicted him," release on parole, and only years later "an absolute pardon, which acknowledged that Washington was wrongfully convicted."
items.reading: A quick second round of clarification, outside review or quiet policy change, or the matter simply fading.
items.loss: The decades-long, step-by-step path to vindication, depending on successive governors' discretion rather than courts or public pressure, is missed.

items.record: The true perpetrator was eventually identified: "Kenneth Tinsley... pleaded guilty to Rebecca Lynn Williams' rape and murder."
items.reading: Says it cannot know whether the fringe claim is true.
items.loss: The decisive confirmation that the official account was wrong, and who actually committed the crime, is absent.

items.record: The wronged man's own response was mild and grateful: "This was a whole lot better than I expected."
items.reading: Critics feel erased by a press release, told politely that their experience does not count.
items.loss: The emotional stance of the wrongly convicted person (understated relief rather than grievance at being dismissed) is misdescribed.

items.record: The victim's last words framed the investigation: she "could only describe her attacker as a Black man acting alone," and police later pinned the crime on a man arrested for unrelated offenses.
items.loss: The origin of the wrongful case (a vague, race-based description plus opportunistic attribution to someone already in custody) is missing.
